title: Palantir Guided for $2.16 Billion in Revenue for Q3. Its Last 2 Quarters Suggest We Should Expect More.

Palantir Guided for $2.16 Billion in Revenue for Q3. Its Last 2 Quarters Suggest We Should Expect More.

PLTR
NVDA

Trading disclosure

Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR) has been one of the biggest winners of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, with its stock gaining more than 1,000% over the last three years. But investors who think the company's best days are behind it may be in for a surprise when Palantir reports its third-quarter results on Nov. 2.

That's because Palantir has developed a habit of beating its own revenue guidance -- and its margins are widening.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The company's guidance was for third-quarter revenue between $2.160 billion and $2.164 billion, which would amount to another impressive quarter of growth. But based on Palantir's performances in the first half of the year, I think that forecast is far too conservative.

In fact, I wouldn't be surprised if Palantir delivers more than $2.3 billion in revenue, easily surpassing its own expectations.

Here's why.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
Palantir keeps raising the bar

Palantir has been on an incredible run this year, fueled by demand for its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP), which helps businesses and government agencies analyze enormous amounts of information and use AI to make decisions.

But what's particularly interesting is how Palantir consistently underestimates its own growth. When the company issued its first-quarter guidance in February, it projected revenue between $1.532 billion and $1.536 billion. Instead, it delivered $1.633 billion -- about 6.4% above the midpoint of that range.

The second quarter's beat was even better. Management projected revenue between $1.797 billion and $1.801 billion, but Palantir generated $1.935 billion -- approximately 7.5% more than projected.

The company's growth is accelerating, too. Revenue increased 16% sequentially in the first quarter, followed by a 19% increase in the second quarter. Year-over-year revenue growth reached 93% in Q2, up from 85% in Q1.

Now look at the company's third-quarter guidance.

Palantir's forecast of approximately $2.16 billion represents sequential growth of just under 12%. That would be a significant slowdown in growth from the previous quarter.

That doesn't make much sense to me, particularly when Palantir's commercial business has been expanding so rapidly. If the company simply matches its second-quarter sequential growth rate of 19%, third-quarter revenue would reach approximately $2.3 billion. And I think there's a reasonable chance Palantir will do even better.

By John Jannarone

CorpGov's IPO Edge recently sat down to speak with both Andy Boyd, CEO of REDLattice and Eli Baker, CEO of Bold Eagle Acquisition Corp. (Nasdaq: BEAG) as a followup to an interview at Nasdaq with Mr. Boyd earlier this month. The two entities are combining to take REDLattice public in a deal expected to close around the end of this year. Below are additional questions that didn't make it into the original Nasdaq interview, giving investors a deeper look at REDLattice.

Additionally, while Mr. Boyd and Mr. Baker couldn't comment on any financial guidance, IPO Edge reviewed REDLattice's investor presentation which provides details that help build a valuation analysis. Defense tech and security stocks have traded off recently, but we think the shares can trade into the low-to-mid teens based on backlog growth which creates visibility into 2027 and beyond. It's also worth noting that AE Industrial Partners, the private equity firm that's a current owner of REDLattice, is rolling all of its equity into the public company. AE and the SPAC sponsor, Eagle Equity Partners, together will invest another $60 million of cash into the transaction at $10 per share – an unusually strong vote of confidence.

Here are some key highlights that stood out to us:

In 2025 the company converted approximately 29% of its year-end 2024 pipeline of $838 million into revenue.

As the backlog grows, it's likely that conversion ratio declines somewhat due to revenue recognition issues and multi-year contract terms. But assuming a conversion ratio of about 25% applied to a year-end 2025 pipeline of $1.2 billion, IPO Edge forecasts $300 million in revenue in 2026. At REDLattice's own forecasted margins of ~24%, Ebitda should reach about $75 million in 2026.

Backlog continues to grow, reaching $1.5 billion at the end of the second quarter. Assuming continued backlog growth for the rest of this year plus comparable conversion and margins, IPO Edge expects $85-95 million of Ebitda in 2027.

REDLattice's most comparable peer is Cellebrite (Nasdaq: CLBT), which trades around 15x 2027 EBITDA, but isn't growing anywhere near as fast. It's also worth pointing out similarities to Palantir Technologies Inc. (Nasdaq: PLTR), which commands a multiple of more-than 60 times 2027 Ebitda.

Conservatively applying a multiple of 16-18 times to our estimate of $85-95 million in 2027 Ebitda, we arrive at an enterprise value of at least $1.5 billion compared with the value of $1.25 billion assigned in the Bold Eagle – REDLattice merger at $10 a share.

Last week, the artificial intelligence trade had its roughest week in months, and it was not just one company's problem. A hot inflation report raised the odds that borrowing costs will stay expensive, Goldman Sachs (NYSE: GS) and its CEO warned about debt piling up behind data center build-outs, and the selling spread quickly.

Oracle fell about 9%. Advanced Micro Devices dropped a similar amount. Super Micro Computer lost 23% and was the worst stock in the S&P 500. Palantir Technologies slid into correction territory as AI software names shed roughly $260 billion in value. CoreWeave and its $50 billion in debt made the headlines, but the damage extended to companies with no debt at all.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

That is where the opportunity is.

Image source: Getty Images.
Why Astera Labs got caught in the AI sell-off

Astera Labs (NASDAQ: ALAB) fell over 15% last week, and nothing about its business changed. The company makes the connectivity chips that sit between GPUs, CPUs, and memory inside AI servers, the retimers, switches, and cable modules that keep signals clean as data moves faster. If you think of a GPU as the engine, Astera makes the wiring harness. When investors dump anything tied to data center spending, Astera goes with it, even though it has no borrowings and about $1.25 billion in cash and short-term investments.

The sell-off was about who can afford to keep building. Astera is not the one borrowing.

What Astera Labs did this fall while the market panicked

The reason to buy this dip rather than any other one is what the company shipped in the weeks around it. On Oct. 8, Astera announced Aries 7, which it calls the industry's first full lineup of PCIe 7 signal-conditioning chips spanning both copper and optical links. PCIe 7 is the next-generation standard for moving data between chips, and Astera's parts now cover everything from a few centimeters of circuit board to more than 50 meters of fiber between racks. Intel and AMD, which have both validated Astera's retimers since PCIe 4, are collaborating with the company on the PCIe 7 transition. Samples ship this quarter.

Four days later, at the Open Compute Project summit, Astera unveiled Orion, a rack-scale reference design that lets a cloud provider pick whichever GPU or CPU is cheapest or most available and swap it later without redesigning the rack. It scales to 160 accelerators per pod and is built for neoclouds and enterprises serving AI inference.

Palantir's growth has been impressive

Palantir's AI-powered data analytics software has become more popular over the past two decades. It started as a government-focused company, providing software to various government entities. This eventually expanded into the commercial sector, where it's seeing the fastest growth today. Still, government revenue accounts for more than half of Palantir's total revenue.

Palantir's strength lies in its ability to work within existing systems and deliver actionable insights quickly. This can work in a fully automated environment or with human intervention as the final approval before an action is performed. Palantir has become a popular way for businesses across industries to integrate AI into their existing systems, and this shows up in its financials.

During the second quarter, its U.S. commercial revenue grew at a breathtaking 149% pace, while U.S. government revenue increased 90%. Overall, Palantir's revenue rose 93% year over year to $1.94 billion. That overall figure is important to note because Palantir only guided for about $1.8 billion in Q2 revenue. That's a significant beat, but Palantir has been underguiding and overdelivering for some time.

For Q3, management expects revenue of $2.16 billion. That projects an 83% revenue growth rate, which would be a deceleration from Q2's level. However, if Palantir beats revenue expectations by a similar amount to Q2 (about $150 million), that would boost Palantir's growth rate to 96%, allowing it to continue reporting accelerating revenue growth.

It's important that Palantir does this because its valuation suggests that it needs to continue doubling each year.

Cathie Wood, head of Ark Investment Management, often takes profits when her favorite tech stocks rally.

That's what she's been doing with Palantir Technologies (PLTR), selling shares as the stock rallies ahead of its third-quarter earnings report.

Last year, the flagship Ark Innovation ETF gained 35.49%, far outpacing the S&P 500's return of 17.88% in the same period. So far this year, Wood's flagship Ark Innovation ETF (ARKK) is up 11.05% as of Oct. 21, while the S&P 500 surged 13.32%, Yahoo Finance data shows.

Wood gained a reputation after the Ark Innovation ETF delivered a rosy 153% return in 2020. But her style also brings painful losses in bearish markets, as seen in 2022, when the ETF tumbled more than 60%.

Those swings have weighed on Wood's long-term gains. As of Oct. 21, her Ark Innovation ETF has delivered a five-year annualized return of -6.36%, while the S&P 500 has an annualized return of 11.26% over the same period, according to data from Morningstar.

Cathie Wood remains optimistic about AI and tech revolution

Wood focuses on high-tech companies across artificial intelligence, blockchain, biomedical technology, and robotics. She believes these businesses have strong growth potential, but their volatility often causes fluctuations in the Ark's funds.

Over the decade ended 2025, the Ark Innovation ETF wiped out nearly $5 billion in investor wealth, according to a report by Morningstar's analyst Amy Arnott. That made it the fourth-biggest wealth destroyer among mutual funds and ETFs in the ranking. 

Wood defended her investment strategy after an audience member at a recent summit questioned ARK's performance compared with the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ).

Related: Cathie Wood buys $11.8 million of tumbling tech stock

"I welcome the question. Investors deserve to understand both their returns and the decisions behind them," Wood said in a post on X on Oct. 5.

She argued that the ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK) and QQQ are built differently. QQQ tracks the Nasdaq-100 Index, while ARK actively invests in companies it believes are driving disruptive innovation across industries including healthcare, financial services and transportation.

Wood has long been optimistic about AI, which she sees as a major driver of productivity, economic growth, and corporate profits in the years ahead. She has also pushed back against recent fears that AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.

In September, Wood reposted a post by David Sacks on X, saying he makes a good case that the "AI will kill humanity" headlines were orchestrated.

title: What Palantir Technologies Holders Got Right

What Palantir Technologies Holders Got Right
Bailey Pemberton
Thu, October 22, 2026 at 9:15 AM MST 4 min read
PLTR
Trade PLTR on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

If Palantir Technologies sat on your watchlist instead of in your holdings, the move over the past few months may feel like a missed shot. Holding Palantir Technologies from the start of the year would have returned 20.2%, including dividends. The obvious question is what, back on 1 January 2026, could have helped you judge whether its AI-powered data platforms and government contracts were strong enough to justify those rich profit margin assumptions baked into bullish models.

A Narrative on Simply Wall St is one investor's written case for a company, with its growth, margin and multiple assumptions spelled out. Those assumptions imply an estimated Fair Value.

The move put Palantir Technologies in the middle of this trade. Scan 55 AI infrastructure stocks for other companies exposed to it.

What Palantir Investors Were Really Arguing About

The shares cost US$178 at the start of the period, which forced anyone watching Palantir Technologies to decide whether that price matched the story they believed.

On the bullish side, one narrative put Fair Value at US$440, or 148% above the start price. This view was based on Palantir reaching 32.0% revenue growth with profit margins of 18.0% over a 10-year stretch.

The more cautious view set Fair Value at US$19.79. Its author assumed 29.0% revenue growth, 14.0% profitability and a future P/E of 55.0x over 5 years as a risk aware path.

NasdaqGS:PLTR Trailing 12-Month Earnings & Revenue History as at Oct 2026
What The Evidence Did To The Palantir Technologies Debate

Palantir Technologies reported Q2 2026 revenue of US$1.94b and net income of US$1.06b, with net margin rising to 54.9%, which supported the optimistic case on growth and profitability. At the same time, repeated references to premium valuation multiples, insider selling in the hundreds of millions, and a P/E still described as expensive kept the cautious view about pricing alive. Overall, the evidence cut both ways.

The whole argument turned on whether rich margin and growth assumptions would show up in audited numbers. For any other stock, track multi quarter revenue, absolute profit and net margin against the story, then ask whether the P/E you are paying already assumes more.

What Palantir's Current Price Already Assumes

Today Palantir Technologies trades at US$202, up from US$178 from the start of the year. The selected Narrative's Fair Value sits below that quote, which frames the stock as already pricing in a strong execution story.

That Narrative leans on Palantir's AI platforms, government roots and commercial traction. Anyone paying today's price is effectively assuming high growth and wide margins persist. The question then becomes how valuation risks in the Narrative shape that bet.

Wall Street did much of the lifting, and a 7% software rout mid-month didn't stick. But the stock now sits almost right on the Street's average price target.

Most of the gain came in early October. Within about two days, Daniel Ives's Yorkville Ives & Co started coverage at Buy with a $250 target, Goldman Sachs upgraded the stock to Buy at $230, and Barclays started at Buy with a $265 target, the Street's highest.

A 7% drop that had nothing to do with Palantir
